title: Managing Stress: Evidence-Based Techniques
content:
Stress is the body's response to any demand or challenge. Short-term stress can be adaptive — sharpening focus and mobilising energy. Chronic stress, however, is linked to physical health problems including high blood pressure, heart disease, obesity, and diabetes, as well as mental health problems including anxiety and depression.

The stress response involves the release of adrenaline (epinephrine) and cortisol, which raise heart rate, blood pressure, and blood glucose. In chronic stress, persistently elevated cortisol can suppress immune function, impair memory, and disrupt sleep.

Evidence-based stress management techniques include:

Diaphragmatic (belly) breathing activates the parasympathetic nervous system, counteracting the stress response. Try inhaling slowly for 4 counts, holding for 4, and exhaling for 6–8 counts. Even a few minutes can produce a measurable reduction in heart rate.

Mindfulness meditation involves focusing attention on the present moment — typically on the breath or bodily sensations — without judgement. A 2014 meta-analysis in JAMA Internal Medicine found mindfulness-based programmes produced modest improvement in anxiety, depression, and pain.

Regular physical activity is one of the most robustly supported stress-reduction tools. Exercise increases endorphins and reduces levels of stress hormones. Even a 20–30 minute walk can improve mood.

Social support — spending time with trusted friends or family, or talking about stressors — is consistently associated with better stress coping. Isolation tends to amplify perceived stress.

Time-structuring strategies, including breaking tasks into smaller steps, prioritising, and scheduling regular breaks, can reduce the sense of being overwhelmed.

If stress is significantly affecting your daily functioning, sleep, or physical health, speaking with a mental health professional is recommended. Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) has strong evidence for reducing stress, anxiety, and depression.
source: Original — based on NIH National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health guidance (public domain) and peer-reviewed literature summaries
